hints: Look carefully at what each bracket covers in the diagram. J covers only the double ring on the left, K covers only the 5-sided sugar in the middle, and L covers all three ovals on the right.
Remember that adenosine already means base plus sugar together, so J alone cannot be adenosine. Also recall ATP uses ribose, a pentose sugar, plus three phosphate groups.
walkthrough:
**Read the diagram like a map**

Look at the three parts. J is the double-ring base. K is the 5-carbon sugar ring. L is the chain of three small ovals.

So we need: base, sugar, three phosphates.

**Apply the ATP recipe**

ATP = adenine + ribose + three phosphates.

Adenine is a double-ring base, which belongs to the purine family. Ribose is a 5-carbon sugar, which belongs to the pentose family.

**Check the names carefully**

J alone is just the base, not base plus sugar, so it cannot be called adenosine. L shows three units, so it must be phosphates (plural), not a single phosphate group and not just the element phosphorus.

Only the general but accurate set purine, pentose, phosphates fits all three brackets.

options.A: Deoxyribose is wrong here. ATP always contains the pentose ribose, not deoxyribose which is found in DNA.
options.B: J alone is only the base, while adenosine means adenine plus ribose together. L is also three phosphates, not a single phosphate group.
options.C: J is wrong for the same reason, adenosine includes K as well. L is wrong because the units are phosphate groups, not atoms of the element phosphorus.
options.D: Lovely fit. Adenine is a purine base, ribose is a pentose sugar, and L shows three phosphates. General names but all biologically correct.
